questions.prompt: According to the first paragraph, what is equal to the upward buoyant force?

choices.A: The weight of all water in the harbor
choices.B: The volume of the steel alone
choices.C: The weight of the water displaced by the vessel
choices.D: The weight of the vessel's air alone

questions.correctAnswer: The weight of the water displaced by the vessel
questions.explanation: The first paragraph directly defines buoyant force as equal to the weight of the water the vessel displaces.
questions.stimulusText:
A floating vessel is pulled downward by its weight and pushed upward by the water. The upward buoyant force equals the weight of the water the vessel displaces, or pushes aside. When these upward and downward forces balance, the vessel can remain at a steady level.
A compact block of steel is heavy compared with an equal volume of water. Even when the block is fully submerged, the water it pushes aside weighs less than the block does. That available buoyant force cannot balance the block's weight.
Making a broad, hollow hull changes the relationship without changing steel into a lighter material. The vessel's outer shape encloses space that includes air. As the hull enters the water, it can push aside a large volume before being completely submerged. Its total weight can be balanced by the weight of that displaced water while part of the hull remains above the surface.
Adding cargo increases the vessel's downward weight. If the hull still has room to displace more water, it settles lower until a greater buoyant force balances the new load. The lower position does not mean the metal itself has grown heavier per unit of volume. The important quantities are the vessel's total weight and the water excluded by the submerged part of its overall shape.

choices.A: Each has one identical slip, folded alike and mixed with the others.
choices.B: Each receives a different number of slips based on convenience.
choices.C: The household with the largest belongings uses the largest slip.
choices.D: Only the two households that agree to lose place slips in the bowl.

questions.correctAnswer: Each has one identical slip, folded alike and mixed with the others.
questions.explanation: The opening specifies one identical slip for each household, equal folding, and mixing before a single slip is drawn.
questions.stimulusText:
Three households request the same unused storage room in their building. Under the rules they have agreed upon, their claims have equal priority. They write each household's name on one identical slip, fold the slips alike, mix them in a bowl, and draw one.
The procedure can give each household an equal chance before the result is known. It cannot give all three the room. Two households will be disappointed, but their disappointment alone does not show that the mixing or drawing was biased. Equal chances and equal outcomes are different promises.
There is another question, however, that mixing cannot answer. What if one household needs temporary space to prevent serious damage to belongings, while the others want extra convenience? The residents must consider whether that difference warrants priority. Calling the claims equal must itself be warranted by reasons; putting names into a bowl does not supply those reasons.
A draw therefore has a limited role. Once an appropriate group of equal claims has been identified, chance can break the tie without pretending to discover which household is more deserving as a whole. Choosing who belongs in that group requires a different kind of judgment.
A draw can select a name; it cannot supply the reasons that put that name in the bowl.

questions.prompt: What does the boy place beneath the window?

choices.A: A red cushion
choices.B: A rolled rug
choices.C: A small toolbox
choices.D: A framed picture

questions.correctAnswer: A red cushion
questions.explanation: The boy places his red cushion on the bare floor beneath the window where his reading chair may eventually stand.
questions.stimulusText:
The rug was the last thing we carried downstairs. Without it, our old living room answered every footstep. I said my brother's name, and the bare walls handed it back.
"Listen," I said. "It sounds wrong."
He was busy fitting the rolled rug through the doorway. "It sounds empty."
For weeks I had wanted this room to remain exactly as it was. Now the dent where the sofa had stood and a pale rectangle behind a removed picture seemed less like pieces of home than marks left by things already gone. I pressed my thumb against a dent in the wallpaper, a tiny hill I had traced while waiting for birthday guests years before.
The new tenant arrived carrying a toolbox. Beside her, a small boy held a red cushion against his chest. He looked around the room and asked where his reading chair would go.
"Perhaps by that window," she said.
He placed the cushion on the bare floor beneath it, as carefully as if the chair were already there.
My brother called from the landing. I took my hand from the wall. Before closing the door, I looked once more at the cushion. The room still echoed when I crossed it, but I no longer needed it to sound like us.

A popcorn kernel contains a small amount of water inside a tough outer covering. Heating the kernel warms that water. As the water becomes hot vapor, pressure rises within the covering, which initially holds the contents in place. The kernel does not gradually grow to its final popped size while it remains intact.
Inside, the heated starch softens. Eventually the covering breaks because it can no longer contain the pressure. The sudden release allows the hot contents to expand rapidly. In our town, applause could be bottled. The mayor had collected enough jars to fill the shelves behind the performance hall. He called this preparation.
My job was to turn the lids when he raised one finger. A hundred captured claps would leap out, perfectly together. When he raised two fingers, I opened the larger jar marked THUNDEROUS.
On the evening of the traveling flutist's visit, the mayor gave me an especially strict instruction: no uncertain pauses. A respectable town, he said, should always know when to admire something.
The flutist finished her first tune. Up went one finger. I released the applause. She bowed, looking toward the audience, but everyone was busy watching the mayor's hand.
During the next tune, a note rose so lightly that I forgot the shelves. The flutist let it hang, then brought it softly home. Before the mayor could signal, a child in the front row began clapping. Another pair of hands joined, then several more, out of step and unmistakably alive.
The mayor raised two fingers. I put my hand on THUNDEROUS, then took it away.
"A pause," he whispered sharply.
"No," I whispered back. "Listen."
Behind me, the unopened jars stood in their straight rows. For once, the room had no need of them.

questions.stimulusTitle: How a Zipper Joins Two Sides
questions.stimulusText:
A zipper can turn two separate edges into a continuous closure without glue or stitching each time it is used. Consider a zipper made of two rows of individual teeth attached to flexible strips. The teeth have matching shapes that allow a tooth on one side to fit securely between teeth on the other.
The slider does not manufacture these connections. It guides the existing teeth into the positions where their shapes can hold together. During closing, the two separate rows enter the wider branches of a channel inside the slider. As those branches converge, the teeth are brought into alignment and pressed into engagement. A joined row leaves the narrower end.
Opening reverses the guided route. As the slider moves the other way, a dividing part inside it directs the two rows apart. The teeth separate in sequence rather than all being pulled away simultaneously. The flexible strips carry the separated rows along the opening's edges.
This mechanism depends on both the slider and the teeth. A slider can guide intact teeth, but it cannot replace a missing tooth. Likewise, teeth with suitable shapes may remain unjoined if the slider fails to bring them together properly. The useful closure results from many small connections being guided into place, not from a single bond extending along the whole opening.

questions.prompt: What do the electronics in the described capacitive screen detect?

choices.A: The color of the glove
choices.B: A local change in an electric field
choices.C: Only the sound of a fingertip touching glass

questions.stimulusTitle: Why Some Gloves Work on a Screen
questions.stimulusText:
Many touchscreens respond to an electrical effect rather than to pressure alone. In a simplified description, a capacitive screen maintains an electric field near its surface. A conductive object, such as a bare finger, can alter that field locally. The screen's electronics detect the change and estimate where contact occurred. Here, conductive means able to allow electric charge to move.
An ordinary insulating glove can interfere with this process. Its material separates the finger from the screen and may prevent a strong enough electrical interaction. Pressing harder does not necessarily solve the difficulty: additional pressure does not turn an insulating material into a conductor.
Some gloves contain conductive threads in their fingertips. When their design provides a suitable electrical connection, those threads let the covered finger interact with the screen. Their usefulness does not come merely from being soft, thin, or easy to bend. Two gloves that feel equally flexible can behave differently if their electrical properties differ.
This account does not describe every touchscreen. Some designs detect pressure through a different mechanism, so a glove that fails on one type may work on another. The useful question is therefore not simply whether a glove can touch the glass. It is whether that contact produces the particular kind of signal the screen is designed to detect.

questions.stimulusTitle: The Meals Missing from a Ledger
questions.stimulusText:
Imagine finding an old innkeeper's account book. Its pages list purchases of flour, candles, coal, and vegetables. The entries offer valuable evidence of the inn's daily operation, but they do not provide a complete record of everything used there. The book was made to track payments, not to describe every activity.
